title: The preliminaries
hook: first point: the four thoughts that turn the mind

segments.voice: Yesterday, lojong: Chekawa's seven points of mind training. Your line was seven points. Can you still count them off on your fingers? Today, point one. Day one thousand two hundred ninety-seven.

Onions first. Before anything goes in the pan, the cook peels, chops, measures, sets out the salt. Nobody posts a photo of that part. It's slow and it smells and it isn't the dish. But skip it, and the dish falls apart halfway through, with something burning while you hunt for the garlic. Mind training opens the same way. Before the famous practices, before the slogans about dreams and patience, the very first line of the text says, in effect, start with the groundwork. Today, point one of seven: the preliminaries.
screen: `ONIONS FIRST.` → `SKIP IT AND THE DISH FALLS APART.` → `POINT ONE: THE GROUNDWORK.`

segments.voice: First, the slogan. The opening line of the seven points is usually given as: first, train in the preliminaries. The whole rest of the text stands on them. Second, what the preliminaries are. Tibetan commentaries explain them as four thoughts that turn the mind. One: this human life is precious and hard to come by. Two: it will end, and nobody knows when. Three: actions have results, and they follow you. Four: the round of samsara, however you rearrange it, doesn't satisfy. Third, if that sounds familiar, it should. Last week the lamrim walked through these same four, a day each. Here they come back, packed tight, as the ground floor of mind training. That repetition is the point. Tibetan teachers say a student doesn't graduate from the preliminaries; the basics get revisited at the start of a session, the start of a day, the start of a hard week. Fourth, why they turn the mind. Picture a cart rolling one way out of habit: toward comfort, distraction, more of the same. The four thoughts are a hand on the shaft, turning it. Not by force, but by seeing clearly. If life is precious, short, consequential and not fixable by rearranging, then, in this teaching, training the heart stops looking like a hobby. Only after that turn does Chekawa's text go on to the main practice, and tomorrow, so do we.
screen: `FIRST, TRAIN IN THE PRELIMINARIES.` · `FOUR THOUGHTS THAT TURN THE MIND.` · `THE LAMRIM'S WEEK, PACKED TIGHT.` · `A HAND ON THE CART, TURNING IT.` · then, large: `FIRST THE BASICS.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: recall the four thoughts. Sit and let the breath settle. Then give each thought a few slow breaths. This life: precious, rare, here right now. This life: it will end, time unknown. What I do: it has results. The round: rearranging it doesn't satisfy. Don't argue with them or polish them. Let each one land, like setting out ingredients on the counter. Then sit with all four in front of you, and notice whether anything in you turns, even slightly. The bell holds the time.
The preliminaries. The first of the seven points: four thoughts that turn the mind, the groundwork for everything after. Today's word.

Your line: first the basics. Today, before you start one task, pause and pick one of the four thoughts to start with. Precious, short, consequential, unsatisfying. Day one thousand two hundred ninety-seven.

howItsDone: Tibetan Buddhist practitioners often begin a session by bringing to mind the four thoughts that turn the mind: precious human life, death and impermanence, karma, and the faults of samsara.
